newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Sweeping pact to free up telecoms trade clinched.
newsitem.headline: Sweeping pact to free up telecoms trade clinched.

text.p: Sixty-eight countries agreed on Saturday to a sweeping pact that will open up the world's $600 billion telecommunications market to competition and give a big boost to the industry and the information superhighway.
Delegations inside the meeting hall clapped when the chairman of the World Trade Organisation-sponsored talks announced a deal was cut just hours before a midnight Geneva time (2300 GMT) deadline.
"We've got an agreement. We are all very happy," a Latin American trade ambassador said.
A WTO official added: "It has been concluded successfully. The agreement is done."
The breakthrough to the lengthy negotiations came after the United States, the world's biggest telecoms market and key to a deal, eased its position on Friday after months of tough negotiating.
U.S. industry and congressional groups immediately welcomed the deal, which is also seen as a big boost to the credibility of the fledgling, two-year-old WTO.

"We commend the WTO for its work in getting us an international trade agreement that opens markets and increases foreign investment," the Global Information Infrastructure Commission, a broad U.S. telecoms industry coalition, said in a statement.
"This agreement lays the foundation for significant new investment in informatics and telecommunications infrastructure in nations around the world," it added.
The pact on basic telecoms would for the first time bring under WTO's umbrella services such as satellite systems, cellular phones, data transmission and paging.
This would also mean stability for foreign investors, with an accord placing foreign participation issues under WTO's binding commitments.
In Washington, House Commerce Committee chairman Tom Bliley hailed the pact as a big victory for the U.S. telecoms market.

"The real winners today are American communications workers who'll soon enyoy an expansion of high-paying, high-technology jobs as America begins to export our state-of-the-art technology to the global marketplace," he said in a statement.
The agreement was expected to be announced also in Washington by U.S. Trade Representative-designate Charlene Barshefsky, her office said.
The new pact would boost the $600 billion telecoms industry, already one of the most dynamic in the world, according to the United Nations International Telecommunications Union (ITU).
An ITU survey predicted on Friday that world revenues from the industry, including that from equipment, could almost double to more than $1.2 trillion by the year 2000 if a deal is struck.
European Union Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said the pact would slash telephone costs for ordinary people and businesses around the globe and speed up the digital revolution.
"A WTO deal on telecoms services today will give a powerful lift to the globalisation of telecoms markets," he said earlier.
"In addition to what this deal will do for the telecoms industry, it is a major step also in the creation of the information society."
Washington walked away from a deal last year, saying offers, particularly from emerging nations, were not good enough.
This time round, it had strongly criticised Canada's cap on foreign equity ownership in domestic telecoms companies.

A U.S. official said there had been intensive discussions overnight with the Canadian negotiators. On Friday, Washington said it would add curbs on satellite transmission of some television and audio services to its offer on the table, which trade diplomats said were primarily aimed at Ottawa.
WTO Director-General Renato Ruggiero has set success in the talks, left over from the 1986-93 Uruguay Round of world trade negotiations, as top priority for the body.
